Comprehensive DApp Testing Strategies
Build, validate, and integrate program and client tests so your DApp is secure and reliable.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Practice Checklist
Test Accounts & PDAs
Generate test Keypairs and compute PDAs with the same seeds your program expects. This gives deterministic access to test accounts and simplifies assertions across runs.
Example
Use Keypair.generate() for ephemeral accounts, and PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync to compute PDAs used by the program.
Tip
Reset the local validator between runs for deterministic state when debugging failing tests.
E2E Flow Checklist
Your E2E should navigate to the DApp, connect a simulated wallet or mock it, perform the action (initialize or increment), approve the transaction, and assert the UI update. If simulating wallets is complex, mock the connection and focus on UI and serialization correctness.
Common Scenario
Mint or increment flows where user clicks a button, approves a transaction, and the UI displays the new state.
Why it helps
E2E tests catch UI serialization issues, incorrect deserialization of account data, and integration gaps between wallet prompts and your client code.

screens.title: Local Validator: fast, isolated testing
screens.narratorSegment: A local validator is the fastest way to validate program logic without paying fees or incurring network delays. Running solana-test-validator launches a private, isolated cluster that mimics transaction processing, account storage, and program execution. That determinism makes it ideal for automated tests and quick iterations. A concrete example: when you run anchor test, Anchor often starts a local validator, deploys the program, and runs your test cases against it. This means you can create Keypairs, compute PDAs, call initialize instructions, and fetch accounts all within milliseconds. A common misconception is that tests on devnet are representative enough; devnet introduces shared state, variable latency, and potential third-party interference. By contrast, a local validator gives you a clean slate for each run and integrates tightly with debugging tools and stack traces. For practical use: start the validator, deploy your program, run your Anchor tests, and reset between failing runs. Key takeaway: build fast feedback loops with the local validator to catch logic errors early and cheaply. Question to reflect on: which failing condition would be easier to reproduce on a local validator than on devnet?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Local Validator
Definition
A local validator is a private Solana cluster that emulates core runtime behavior so you can deploy and test programs offline and without cost.
Why use it
  • Faster iteration and immediate feedback when running tests.
  • Deterministic environment for repeatable failure reproduction.
  • No devnet/mainnet fees or public state interference.
Common mistake
Relying solely on devnet for development testing, which can mask reproducible failures due to shared state or network latency.
Try this
Run solana-test-validator or use anchor test --skip-build --skip-deploy to start a local cluster and run tests locally.
Terminal demo
Example commands and expected quick outputs when starting a local validator and deploying a program for tests.
$ solana-test-validator
# Starts local cluster and logs ledger path and RPC endpoint
$ anchor test
# Anchor deploys to local validator, runs tests, and prints passing test results
Key takeaway
Make the validator the default test backend during development to drastically shorten your debug cycle.

screens.title: Unit Tests with Anchor
screens.narratorSegment: Unit tests verify a single behavior or instruction of your on-chain program in isolation. With Anchor you write JavaScript or TypeScript tests that call a specific instruction, provide accounts and signers, and then assert the expected account state or program error. A classic example is a counter program: write one test to initialize a counter and assert the count is zero, and another that calls increment and checks that the stored value increases. Anchor helps by deploying to the local validator and providing convenient methods like program. methods. initialize(). accounts(...). rpc(). A common misconception is treating unit tests like full system tests; they should be small and deterministic, focusing on a single instruction or state change. For robust coverage add negative tests that expect failure when an unauthorized user signs, or when inputs are out of range. These unit tests are fast and should run in CI. Practice exercise: write an Anchor test using Keypair. generate() for the counter account and assert count equals zero after initialization. Unit Tests with Anchor means test individual instructions with targeted inputs and explicit assertions, including negative cases for access control.. In practical terms, writing focused tests for individual instructions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Anchor Unit Tests
What to test
  • Instruction success paths: expected state changes after a call.
  • Negative paths: unauthorized signer, invalid inputs, or missing accounts.
  • Boundary values: zero, maximum integers, and empty inputs.
Misconception
Unit tests are not integration tests; they should remain focused and fast so they can run often in CI.
Concrete example
// Example: Anchor test for a counter program
import * as anchor from "@project-serum/anchor";
import { Program } from "@project-serum/anchor";
import { Counter } from "../target/types/counter"; // Your program's type definitions
import { assert } from "chai";

describe("counter", () => {
  const provider = anchor.AnchorProvider.env();
  anchor.setProvider(provider);

  const program = anchor.workspace.Counter as Program<Counter>;
  let counterAccount = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate();

  it("Is initialized!", async () => {
    const payer = provider.wallet.publicKey;

    await program.methods
      .initialize()
      .accounts({
        counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
        user: payer,
        systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
      })
      .signers([counterAccount])
      .rpc();

    const account = await program.account.counter.fetch(counterAccount.publicKey);
    assert.equal(account.count.toNumber(), 0);
  });
});
Support cards
Example assertion
Use assert.equal(account.count.toNumber(), expected) to compare numeric state after a transaction.
Pitfall
Forgetting to sign with a created Keypair when creating accounts can cause unexpected authorization errors during tests.
Key Takeaway
Keep unit tests small, deterministic, and fast so they run frequently and inform development decisions.

screens.title: Integration Tests with Anchor
screens.narratorSegment: Integration tests validate how different instructions and accounts interact across a sequence of calls. For example, an integration test might initialize a counter, perform several increment calls, and then assert the final state. Unlike focused unit tests, integration tests confirm that your program behaves correctly when instructions are executed in order and when multiple accounts change together. Anchor simplifies this by deploying the program to the local validator and letting your test script orchestrate multiple RPC calls, account creations, and fetches. A concrete integration example: call initialize, then increment twice, and assert the count equals two. A common misconception is treating integration tests as slow and optional; instead, include a small suite of integration tests in CI to catch state-machine bugs and interaction regressions. When writing integration tests, create fresh test accounts or PDAs as needed, and be explicit about signing and payer accounts. End with this practical check: if a sequence sometimes fails only on CI, inspect wallet keys and shared state — the local validator ensures determinism during debugging. Integration Tests with Anchor means exercise multi-step flows to validate combined instruction logic, state transitions, and account interactions.. In practical terms, verify multi-instruction flows and cross-account behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Integration Tests
Step-by-step pattern
1. Prepare accounts
Generate keypairs and compute PDAs used across the flow.
2. Perform sequence
Call initialize, then call subsequent instructions that mutate state.
3. Assert final state
Fetch accounts and assert the cumulative result matches expectations.
Concrete example
Initialize counter, call increment twice, and assert the counter equals two. Integration tests ensure that multiple instructions compose correctly.
Why include integration tests in CI
They catch regressions that arise when interactions change, such as order-dependent state mutations, race conditions in test setup, or incorrect PDA usage across calls.
Misconception
Integration tests do not replace unit tests; they complement them by exercising multi-step behavior that individual tests may miss.
Key Takeaway
Maintain a small but meaningful set of integration tests that run in CI to protect common user flows and state transitions.

screens.title: Counter Test Example — successes and failures
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a complete test scenario for a counter program to demonstrate both success and failure checks. First, generate a counter account keypair and use the provider wallet as payer. Call initialize and fetch the account to assert the count starts at zero. Next, call increment and assert the counter increases by one. Finally, test a negative case by attempting to increment with a different signer; assert that the program throws the expected authorization error. This negative test is important: it proves that access control logic is enforced. A typical failure mode is forgetting to include the correct signer in the signers array, which will either cause an error at the RPC layer or allow an unintended success if access checks are missing. When running these tests, examine the error message — Anchor will often present a constraint violation string that helps pinpoint the failed check. Reflection question: which of these tests would you prioritize if you could only add one test before a release? Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Counter Test Walkthrough
Example test sequence
it("Is initialized!", async () => {
  const payer = provider.wallet.publicKey;

  await program.methods
    .initialize()
    .accounts({
      counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
      user: payer,
      systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
    })
    .signers([counterAccount])
    .rpc();

  const account = await program.account.counter.fetch(counterAccount.publicKey);
  assert.equal(account.count.toNumber(), 0);
});

it("Increments the counter!", async () => {
  await program.methods.increment().accounts({
    counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
    user: provider.wallet.publicKey,
  }).rpc();
  const account = await program.account.counter.fetch(counterAccount.publicKey);
  assert.equal(account.count.toNumber(), 1);
});

it("Fails to increment if wrong user signs", async () => {
  const maliciousUser = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate();
  try {
    await program.methods.increment().accounts({
      counterAccount: counterAccount.publicKey,
      user: maliciousUser.publicKey,
    }).signers([maliciousUser]).rpc();
    assert.fail("Should have failed with unauthorized error");
  } catch (error) {
    assert.include(error.message, "A has_one constraint was violated");
  }
});
Explanation cards
Signing rules
When creating accounts, include the new Keypair in signers. When verifying authorization, test with both valid and invalid signers.
Failure diagnosis
Read Anchor error messages for constraints or custom program errors; they often direct you to the violated check.
Key Takeaway
Negative tests are as important as positive ones; they prove protection logic works when it should reject actions.

screens.title: End-to-End (E2E) Tests for DApps
screens.narratorSegment: End-to-end tests simulate full user journeys through your DApp: the browser interface, wallet connection, transaction approval, and final UI updates tied to on-chain state. Tools like Playwright or Cypress can automate a browser to click buttons, mock or simulate wallet interactions, and assert that the application reacts correctly after a transaction. A concrete E2E example for the counter DApp: launch the page, connect a simulated wallet, click Initialize Counter, approve the transaction, click Increment Counter, approve again, and finally assert the displayed count increased. A common challenge is simulating wallet behavior; many teams either use a Playwright extension for a popular wallet or mock the connection and instrument the client to accept a test signer. E2E tests catch problems unit tests miss: UI serialization errors, DOM updates not reflecting account state, or mismatches between wallet prompts and the client's transaction payload. Key takeaway: E2E tests increase confidence in the user experience but are often heavier — keep a small, focused E2E suite that runs in CI and cover the most critical user paths. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › E2E Tests
E2E checklist
  • Navigate to the DApp and detect UI elements like Connect or Initialize buttons.
  • Connect a simulated wallet or mock the wallet API for predictable behavior.
  • Perform UI actions and approve transactions as the user would.
  • Assert the UI updates to reflect on-chain account changes.
Concrete Playwright snippet
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Counter DApp E2E', () => {
  test('should connect wallet, initialize, and increment counter', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('http://localhost:3000');

    // For simplicity assume wallet is connected or mocked
    console.log("Assuming wallet is connected for E2E test.");

    const initializeButton = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Initialize Counter' });
    if (await initializeButton.isVisible()) {
      await initializeButton.click();
      await page.waitForTimeout(5000);
      expect(page.getByText('Transaction confirmed!')).toBeVisible();
    }

    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Increment Counter' }).click();
    await page.waitForTimeout(5000);
    expect(page.getByText('Transaction confirmed!')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
Practical notes
If real wallet automation is difficult, mock the wallet to validate UI behavior and serialization. Then, add a small manual or instrumented test for real wallet approvals as a separate step.
Key Takeaway
Use E2E tests to validate the full user experience; keep them focused and run them in CI to guard critical flows.

screens.title: Unit vs Integration vs E2E
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the differences between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests helps you place effort where it matters. Unit tests are small, fast, and focused on a single instruction or function; they are ideal for verifying algorithmic correctness and small access checks. Integration tests combine multiple instructions or accounts to validate state transitions and interactions across program components. End-to-end tests emulate a full user journey, including the client, wallet, and program, and reveal integration errors that the other two categories might miss. A concrete rule of thumb: write many unit tests for low-level correctness, a smaller set of integration tests for common flows, and a tiny focused E2E suite covering the most critical user actions. A common misconception is to treat one type as sufficient; instead, these tests complement each other. For example, a serialization mismatch might only appear when the frontend constructs a transaction payload — an E2E test would catch this while a unit test would not. Reflect: what user-facing bug would you most fear — a single-instruction arithmetic error or a UI-to-wallet serialization mismatch? Unit vs Integration vs E2E means many unit tests, some integration tests, and a few targeted e2e tests make an effective and efficient testing strategy.. In practical terms, choose the right test type for the right problem. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing Pipeline & CI Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating tests into Continuous Integration ensures regressions are caught before code merges or deployments. A typical CI flow starts the local validator, installs dependencies, runs Anchor unit and integration tests, then runs a small E2E suite or smoke tests. Because the local validator can run in CI, you can automate the same deterministic test runs used locally. Key benefits include earlier vulnerability detection, consistent test environments, and safer refactoring. A common pitfall is running long E2E suites in every pull request; instead, split the pipeline: run unit and integration tests on every push and schedule heavier E2E suites on nightly runs or gated releases. For security, include tests that exercise critical authorization paths and boundary inputs. When a failure occurs in CI, collect logs from the validator and test runner output to reproduce locally. Final reflection: which tests should block merges in your team — unit, integration, or a curated smoke E2E test? In practical terms, run the validator and tests automatically before merges and deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common Testing Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes teams make when testing Solana DApps. First, failing to test edge cases — zero, maximum values, and empty inputs — leads to production surprises. Second, neglecting negative tests means access controls and error paths remain unverified. Third, relying exclusively on devnet or shared environments hides deterministic bugs and introduces noise from other developers. Fourth, E2E tests that attempt to automate real wallets without proper mocks become brittle and slow. To avoid these pitfalls, design tests that include boundary values, add explicit negative cases expecting authorization failures, and make the local validator the backbone of CI. For E2E, prefer mocking wallet behavior for most automated checks and keep a separate manual or instrumented test for real wallet approval flows. Practically, add a failing test first (test-driven), reproduce the bug locally on the validator, fix it, and then re-run the suite. Closing question: what single missing test could have prevented your last production bug? Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing Pitfalls
List of common mistakes
  • Skipping edge-case tests (zero, max values, empty inputs).
  • Not writing negative tests for unauthorized actions or invalid inputs.
  • Using shared devnet state instead of isolated local validator runs.
  • Trying to automate real wallet flows without mocks, producing brittle E2E tests.
Practical fix
Adopt a test-first habit: write a failing test for the bug you want to prevent, reproduce locally, then implement code changes and re-run tests to confirm the fix.
Mistake to avoid
Relying on manual testing only. Manual checks miss regressions and make releases risky.
Quick wins
  • Add a negative test for unauthorized signer behavior.
  • Include a simple E2E smoke test for the critical user path in CI.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Lab Walkthrough
Anchor test starter
// tests/counter.ts (starter)
import * as anchor from "@project-serum/anchor";
import { Program } from "@project-serum/anchor";
import { Counter } from "../target/types/counter";
import { assert } from "chai";

describe("counter program tests", () => {
  const provider = anchor.AnchorProvider.env();
  anchor.setProvider(provider);

  const program = anchor.workspace.Counter as Program<Counter>;
  const counterAccount = anchor.web3.Keypair.generate();

  it("Initializes the counter to 0", async () => {
    const [pda, _bump] = anchor.web3.PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync(
      [Buffer.from("counter"), provider.wallet.publicKey.toBuffer()],
      program.programId
    );

    await program.methods.initialize().accounts({
      counterAccount: pda,
      user: provider.wallet.publicKey,
      systemProgram: anchor.web3.SystemProgram.programId,
    }).rpc();

    const account = await program.account.counter.fetch(pda);
    assert.equal(account.count.toNumber(), 0);
  });
});
Playwright smoke test
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('should connect wallet, initialize, and increment counter', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://localhost:3000');
  console.log("Assuming wallet is connected for E2E test.");
});
Lab instructions
  1. Create the Anchor tests as shown and run anchor test.
  2. Implement the Playwright smoke test and run npx playwright test after starting your DApp.
  3. If wallet automation is hard, mock the wallet and focus on UI assertions.

fullNarratorScript:
Testing on Solana requires planning and layered checks. In this lesson you will learn how to set up a local validator for fast, cost-free iteration, write unit and integration tests with Anchor to validate program logic, and run end-to-end tests that simulate real user flows with a browser and a simulated wallet. You will see concrete examples for a counter program: how to initialize state, assert expected values, and verify that unauthorized actions fail. We will also cover E2E workflows using Playwright or Cypress and why a CI pipeline that runs all these tests is essential before deployment. Across these techniques you will learn to catch logic bugs early, reproduce failures deterministically, and reduce the risk of irreversible on-chain mistakes. Finally, I’ll point out common testing blind spots — missing edge cases or skipping negative tests — and a practical question to guide your next steps: which test type would uncover a wallet deserialization bug versus a smart contract arithmetic bug?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to set up and use a local Solana validator to test programs without network cost, write unit and integration tests with Anchor that exercise program instructions, and implement end-to-end tests to simulate a full user flow including wallet interactions. You will also understand how a robust testing pipeline contributes to security, reliability, and maintainability, and you will be able to identify common testing scenarios such as edge-case numeric inputs, unauthorized signer checks, and serialization errors. Each objective is framed as a practical skill: you will run the validator, author tests that assert expected account state changes, and create E2E checks that confirm UI updates after on-chain transactions. We will also practice negative tests that assert correct failure modes. Think about which skill you want to apply first — deploying quick Anchor tests or building a Playwright flow — and focus your hands-on work there.

This second objectives screen translates learning goals into practice tasks. You will learn to generate Keypairs for test accounts, locate program-derived addresses for deterministic storage, and write tests that intentionally provoke your program's error paths. You will practice writing an Anchor test that initializes an account and asserts the initial state, and another that increments a counter and verifies the change. We will also cover how to write an assertion that expects an unauthorized signer to fail, so you can confirm access control. Finally, you will set up a basic Playwright E2E that navigates to your DApp, simulates a wallet connection, and verifies UI updates after a transaction. These tasks build confidence: running them repeatedly on a local validator provides a fast feedback loop for correctness and security. Learning Objectives — Practical Focus means convert objectives into repeatable tasks: create accounts, assert state, test failures, and simulate user flows in e2e tests.. In practical terms, hands-on skills and common scenarios to practice. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A local validator is the fastest way to validate program logic without paying fees or incurring network delays. Running solana-test-validator launches a private, isolated cluster that mimics transaction processing, account storage, and program execution. That determinism makes it ideal for automated tests and quick iterations. A concrete example: when you run anchor test, Anchor often starts a local validator, deploys the program, and runs your test cases against it. This means you can create Keypairs, compute PDAs, call initialize instructions, and fetch accounts all within milliseconds. A common misconception is that tests on devnet are representative enough; devnet introduces shared state, variable latency, and potential third-party interference. By contrast, a local validator gives you a clean slate for each run and integrates tightly with debugging tools and stack traces. For practical use: start the validator, deploy your program, run your Anchor tests, and reset between failing runs. Key takeaway: build fast feedback loops with the local validator to catch logic errors early and cheaply. Question to reflect on: which failing condition would be easier to reproduce on a local validator than on devnet?

Unit tests verify a single behavior or instruction of your on-chain program in isolation. With Anchor you write JavaScript or TypeScript tests that call a specific instruction, provide accounts and signers, and then assert the expected account state or program error. A classic example is a counter program: write one test to initialize a counter and assert the count is zero, and another that calls increment and checks that the stored value increases. Anchor helps by deploying to the local validator and providing convenient methods like program. methods. initialize(). accounts(...). rpc(). A common misconception is treating unit tests like full system tests; they should be small and deterministic, focusing on a single instruction or state change. For robust coverage add negative tests that expect failure when an unauthorized user signs, or when inputs are out of range. These unit tests are fast and should run in CI. Practice exercise: write an Anchor test using Keypair. generate() for the counter account and assert count equals zero after initialization. Unit Tests with Anchor means test individual instructions with targeted inputs and explicit assertions, including negative cases for access control.. In practical terms, writing focused tests for individual instructions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Integration tests validate how different instructions and accounts interact across a sequence of calls. For example, an integration test might initialize a counter, perform several increment calls, and then assert the final state. Unlike focused unit tests, integration tests confirm that your program behaves correctly when instructions are executed in order and when multiple accounts change together. Anchor simplifies this by deploying the program to the local validator and letting your test script orchestrate multiple RPC calls, account creations, and fetches. A concrete integration example: call initialize, then increment twice, and assert the count equals two. A common misconception is treating integration tests as slow and optional; instead, include a small suite of integration tests in CI to catch state-machine bugs and interaction regressions. When writing integration tests, create fresh test accounts or PDAs as needed, and be explicit about signing and payer accounts. End with this practical check: if a sequence sometimes fails only on CI, inspect wallet keys and shared state — the local validator ensures determinism during debugging. Integration Tests with Anchor means exercise multi-step flows to validate combined instruction logic, state transitions, and account interactions.. In practical terms, verify multi-instruction flows and cross-account behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a complete test scenario for a counter program to demonstrate both success and failure checks. First, generate a counter account keypair and use the provider wallet as payer. Call initialize and fetch the account to assert the count starts at zero. Next, call increment and assert the counter increases by one. Finally, test a negative case by attempting to increment with a different signer; assert that the program throws the expected authorization error. This negative test is important: it proves that access control logic is enforced. A typical failure mode is forgetting to include the correct signer in the signers array, which will either cause an error at the RPC layer or allow an unintended success if access checks are missing. When running these tests, examine the error message — Anchor will often present a constraint violation string that helps pinpoint the failed check. Reflection question: which of these tests would you prioritize if you could only add one test before a release? Counter Test Example — successes and failures means testing failure cases, such as wrong signer attempts, ensures your program's access controls work as intended.. In practical terms, step through tests that initialize, increment, and assert failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

End-to-end tests simulate full user journeys through your DApp: the browser interface, wallet connection, transaction approval, and final UI updates tied to on-chain state. Tools like Playwright or Cypress can automate a browser to click buttons, mock or simulate wallet interactions, and assert that the application reacts correctly after a transaction. A concrete E2E example for the counter DApp: launch the page, connect a simulated wallet, click Initialize Counter, approve the transaction, click Increment Counter, approve again, and finally assert the displayed count increased. A common challenge is simulating wallet behavior; many teams either use a Playwright extension for a popular wallet or mock the connection and instrument the client to accept a test signer. Understanding the differences between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests helps you place effort where it matters. Unit tests are small, fast, and focused on a single instruction or function; they are ideal for verifying algorithmic correctness and small access checks. Integration tests combine multiple instructions or accounts to validate state transitions and interactions across program components. End-to-end tests emulate a full user journey, including the client, wallet, and program, and reveal integration errors that the other two categories might miss. A concrete rule of thumb: write many unit tests for low-level correctness, a smaller set of integration tests for common flows, and a tiny focused E2E suite covering the most critical user actions. A common misconception is to treat one type as sufficient; instead, these tests complement each other. For example, a serialization mismatch might only appear when the frontend constructs a transaction payload — an E2E test would catch this while a unit test would not. Integrating tests into Continuous Integration ensures regressions are caught before code merges or deployments. A typical CI flow starts the local validator, installs dependencies, runs Anchor unit and integration tests, then runs a small E2E suite or smoke tests. Because the local validator can run in CI, you can automate the same deterministic test runs used locally. Key benefits include earlier vulnerability detection, consistent test environments, and safer refactoring. A common pitfall is running long E2E suites in every pull request; instead, split the pipeline: run unit and integration tests on every push and schedule heavier E2E suites on nightly runs or gated releases. For security, include tests that exercise critical authorization paths and boundary inputs. When a failure occurs in CI, collect logs from the validator and test runner output to reproduce locally. There are several recurring mistakes teams make when testing Solana DApps. First, failing to test edge cases — zero, maximum values, and empty inputs — leads to production surprises. Second, neglecting negative tests means access controls and error paths remain unverified. Third, relying exclusively on devnet or shared environments hides deterministic bugs and introduces noise from other developers. Fourth, E2E tests that attempt to automate real wallets without proper mocks become brittle and slow. To avoid these pitfalls, design tests that include boundary values, add explicit negative cases expecting authorization failures, and make the local validator the backbone of CI. For E2E, prefer mocking wallet behavior for most automated checks and keep a separate manual or instrumented test for real wallet approval flows.
